practice_questions.text:
Where in the female reproductive system does fertilisation normally take place?
A) In the ovary
B) In the uterus
C) In the fallopian tube
D) In the cervix
practice_questions.marks: C) In the fallopian tube [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two functions of the male reproductive system.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: producing sperm / storing sperm (in the epididymis) / delivering sperm (ejaculation) / producing testosterone / producing semen/seminal fluid to nourish sperm. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what happens during ovulation and why it is important for conception.
practice_questions.marks: A basic point scores 1 mark (e.g. 'a mature egg is released from the ovary'). Development scores 2 marks (e.g. 'the egg travels along the fallopian tube where it may be fertilised by sperm'). A further developed answer scores 3 marks by adding specificity (e.g. 'the egg is viable for only 12 to 24 hours after release, so the timing of sexual intercourse relative to ovulation is critical for conception to occur'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the process of fertilisation. Include what happens when a sperm fuses with an egg.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): a single sperm penetrates the egg's outer layer and fuses with it, combining 23 chromosomes from the sperm with 23 chromosomes from the egg to create a zygote with 46 chromosomes (2 marks for clear description of chromosome combination; 1 mark for a basic statement that sperm and egg join). Example/further detail (up to 2 marks): for example, if the sperm carries a Y chromosome the resulting embryo will be male (XY); if it carries an X chromosome the embryo will be female (XX) — sex is determined at the moment of fertilisation. [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A couple have been trying to conceive for several months without success. They understand the basics of reproduction but are unsure about the timing of intercourse in relation to the menstrual cycle.

Discuss the factors related to the menstrual cycle and reproductive biology that affect the likelihood of conception occurring.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two relevant factors. For example: the narrow fertile window around ovulation (approximately six days, with the egg viable for only 12–24 hours), and the role of cycle length variation meaning ovulation does not always fall on day 14. Discussion should also consider that sperm survival (up to five days) means intercourse in the days before ovulation can still result in fertilisation. Both factors should be developed with reasoning linked to the scenario.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two relevant factors identified and briefly explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One factor identified but not clearly explained.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A health educator is preparing a session for teenagers on the biology of reproduction. She wants them to understand the full sequence from ovulation to the establishment of pregnancy.

Evaluate how well an understanding of the menstrual cycle and the stages of conception can support individuals in making informed reproductive choices.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation arguing that knowledge of the cycle (fertile window, ovulation timing, hormone roles) empowers individuals to maximise or minimise the chances of conception through well-timed intercourse or appropriate contraception. This should be challenged by the counter-argument that cycle irregularity, individual variation and medical conditions (e.g. polycystic ovary syndrome) mean biological knowledge alone is insufficient, and professional medical advice remains important. A clear, substantiated judgement is reached.
Secure (5–6 marks): Two or more well-developed points from at least one perspective, with an attempt at a judgement and some reference to limitations.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points identified but largely one-sided or without a clear judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic biological facts stated with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
How much folic acid should a woman take daily when planning a pregnancy?
A) 40 micrograms
B) 400 micrograms
C) 4,000 micrograms
D) 4 grams
practice_questions.marks: B) 400 micrograms [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two reasons why stopping smoking is recommended before trying to conceive.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: smoking reduces sperm count/motility/morphology in men / smoking accelerates egg loss and reduces fertility in women / smoking increases the risk of miscarriage / smoking is linked to earlier menopause / smoking damages the DNA in eggs and sperm. Both must be distinct reasons. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why folic acid is recommended before pregnancy, not just once pregnancy is confirmed.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: folic acid helps prevent neural tube defects / spina bifida. 2 marks: the neural tube forms in the first four weeks after fertilisation, before most women know they are pregnant. 3 marks: by the time a pregnancy is confirmed (often weeks 4-6), the critical window for neural tube development may have already passed, so folic acid must be taken before conception to be effective. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which a man can improve his pre-conception health. Give a reason why each is important.
practice_questions.marks: One factor described with reason = 2 marks; second factor described with reason = 2 marks. Example answers: stop smoking (1 mark) because smoking reduces sperm count and motility, reducing the chance of fertilisation (1 mark); eat a diet rich in zinc and antioxidants (1 mark) because these nutrients support healthy sperm production and quality (1 mark). Other valid factors: reducing alcohol, avoiding excessive heat to the testes, maintaining a healthy weight, stopping recreational drug use. [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A young couple are planning to start a family in the next few months. Neither has visited their GP. The woman smokes occasionally and has not been taking any supplements. The man works long hours and eats few vegetables.

Discuss the pre-conception health changes this couple should make to improve their chances of a healthy pregnancy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): Discussion covers at least two relevant changes for each partner, developed with reasons. For the woman: begin folic acid (400 mcg daily) immediately given the critical neural tube window; stop smoking to protect egg quality and implantation. For the man: improve diet (zinc, antioxidants for sperm quality); consider lifestyle changes given the 74-day sperm maturation timeline. Both sides should be balanced with the scenario context.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two relevant recommendations with brief explanations.
Developing (2 marks): One recommendation with a reason.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point only. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A public health campaign wants to reduce the number of babies born with neural tube defects in the UK.

Evaluate the extent to which improving pre-conception health education for women of childbearing age could reduce the rate of neural tube defects and other pregnancy complications.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation. Arguments for: targeted education about folic acid supplementation (400 mcg ideally from 3 months before conception) could significantly reduce spina bifida rates, given that half of pregnancies are unplanned, meaning many women miss the critical window; education can also address smoking, alcohol and rubella immunity. Counter-argument: barriers include unplanned pregnancies, health literacy gaps, cost of supplements for low-income groups, and the fact that education alone does not change behaviour without structural support (e.g. mandatory fortification of flour, which the UK introduced in 2024). A clear, substantiated judgement is required.
Secure (5–6 marks): At least two points on each side with an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which contraceptive method also provides protection against sexually transmitted infections?
A) The combined contraceptive pill
B) The contraceptive implant
C) The male condom
D) The copper IUD
practice_questions.marks: C) The male condom [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two female causes of infertility.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two distinct answers from: polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) / blocked or damaged fallopian tubes / endometriosis / age-related decline in egg quality / uterine conditions / hormonal imbalance affecting ovulation. Both must be clearly distinct. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how IVF (in vitro fertilisation) helps couples who are unable to conceive naturally.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: IVF involves fertilising an egg with sperm outside the body / in a laboratory. 2 marks: the ovaries are stimulated with hormones to produce multiple eggs, which are collected surgically and fertilised in the laboratory. 3 marks: one or two resulting embryos are transferred to the uterus, bypassing issues such as blocked fallopian tubes or low sperm count that would prevent natural fertilisation. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by an autosomal recessive genetic condition and give one named example.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): an autosomal recessive condition requires a child to inherit one faulty gene copy from each parent in order to be affected; parents who each carry one copy are unaffected carriers (2 marks for a clear description including both inheritance requirement and carrier concept; 1 mark for a basic statement). Example (up to 2 marks): cystic fibrosis is a correct named example (1 mark); explaining that in CF the CFTR gene mutation causes thick mucus to build up in the lungs and digestive system earns a second mark. [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A couple have been told they are both carriers of the sickle cell gene. They are considering their options before starting a family.

Discuss the support available to this couple and the factors they should consider when making decisions about having children.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering the risk (25% chance per pregnancy that the child will be affected), the role of genetic counselling (non-directive, explains options and probabilities), and the reproductive options available (natural conception with prenatal testing, IVF with preimplantation genetic diagnosis, donor gametes, adoption). Discussion should explore the emotional and ethical dimensions as well as the medical facts.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two relevant points explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One point with a brief reason.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A sexual health clinic is reviewing which contraceptive methods to promote most actively in their local area, where rates of chlamydia are significantly above the national average.

Evaluate the extent to which promoting barrier methods of contraception over hormonal methods is the best approach for this clinic to take.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation. Arguments for barrier methods: condoms are the only method that prevents STIs including chlamydia, directly addressing the local problem; barrier methods have no hormonal side effects and are suitable for a wider range of people. Counter-arguments: hormonal methods (pill, implant, injection) are typically more effective at preventing pregnancy; combined promotion (condom + hormonal method) may be the most effective approach for a population with both high STI rates and contraceptive needs; barrier methods have higher typical-use failure rates and require consistent correct use. A clear, substantiated judgement is required.
Secure (5–6 marks): At least two points on each side with an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with little development. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which professional typically leads antenatal care for a low-risk pregnancy in the UK?
A) Obstetrician
B) GP
C) Midwife
D) Health visitor
practice_questions.marks: C) Midwife [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two checks that are carried out at every routine antenatal appointment.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: blood pressure check / urine test (for protein, glucose, bacteria) / weight check / fundal height measurement (from 24 weeks) / foetal heartbeat (from later appointments) / foetal position check (palpation). Both must be distinct. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a screening test and a diagnostic test in antenatal care.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: a screening test identifies risk level / indicates whether further testing is needed. 2 marks: screening cannot confirm whether a condition is present — it gives a statistical risk (e.g. a 1 in 100 chance of Down's syndrome). 3 marks: a diagnostic test such as amniocentesis analyses the baby's actual chromosomes and gives a definitive yes or no answer, but carries a small risk of miscarriage (approximately 0.5%, or 1 in 200, per current NHS guidance), unlike screening tests which are risk-free to the baby. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of the obstetrician in antenatal care. Give one example of a situation where an obstetrician would take the lead.
practice_questions.marks: Role (up to 2 marks): an obstetrician is a hospital-based doctor specialising in pregnancy and birth who takes over or shares care when a pregnancy is classified as high-risk; they monitor and manage complications and may plan or carry out medical interventions such as a caesarean section (2 marks for a clear, developed description; 1 mark for a basic statement). Example (up to 2 marks): for example, if a woman develops gestational diabetes or pre-eclampsia, the obstetrician takes the lead in managing her care, as these conditions can threaten the lives of both mother and baby and require specialist treatment (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague example). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A pregnant woman at 12 weeks receives a result from her combined screening test showing a 1 in 30 risk of Down's syndrome. Her midwife offers her an amniocentesis.

Discuss the factors the woman should consider when deciding whether to have the amniocentesis.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering: the benefit of a definitive result (the amniocentesis will confirm or rule out Down's syndrome, allowing informed planning and access to specialist support); contrasted with the miscarriage risk (approximately 0.5%, or 1 in 200), the emotional stress of the procedure and the wait for results, and the fact that a high-risk screening result does not mean the baby definitely has the condition (1 in 30 means a 97% chance the baby does not). The discussion should acknowledge the non-directive nature of the decision.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two relevant factors explained with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One factor with a brief reason.
Emerging (1 mark): A single point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A community midwifery team is reviewing its booking appointment process after data showed that 20% of women in the area were registering for antenatal care after 12 weeks.

Evaluate the importance of early registration for antenatal care and the consequences of late booking for the health of mother and baby.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation arguing that early registration (ideally by 10 weeks) allows first-trimester screening (nuchal scan, combined blood test) to be completed in time, enables early detection of conditions such as ectopic pregnancy, pre-eclampsia risk factors and anaemia, and gives time for lifestyle interventions. Counter-argument: late booking does not inevitably lead to poor outcomes — many complications can still be identified and managed in the second trimester, and the most damaging complications (e.g. neural tube defects) are influenced by pre-conception health rather than booking timing. Structural barriers to early booking (e.g. women unsure of pregnancy, access issues, language barriers) should be acknowledged. A clear, substantiated judgement is required.
Secure (5–6 marks): At least two well-developed points with an attempt at a judgement.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
During which trimester does organogenesis (the formation of major organs) mainly take place?
A) First trimester (weeks 1-12)
B) Second trimester (weeks 13-27)
C) Third trimester (weeks 28-40)
D) Organogenesis occurs throughout all three trimesters equally
practice_questions.marks: A) First trimester (weeks 1-12) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two benefits for parents of attending antenatal classes.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: increased knowledge of labour stages and pain relief / increased confidence / reduced anxiety / guidance on infant feeding / newborn care skills / social support networks with other expectant parents / partner feels better prepared to support during labour. Both must be distinct. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain what a birth plan is and why it is important in antenatal preparation.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark: a birth plan is a written document setting out a woman's preferences for labour and birth. 2 marks: it covers aspects such as pain relief preferences, who will be present, birth setting, and feeding intentions, and is shared with the midwife in advance. 3 marks: it is important because it ensures the woman's wishes are known and respected as far as possible, even if she is unable to communicate during labour, while also acknowledging that safety takes priority and plans may need to change. [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by the threshold of viability at 24 weeks. Explain one reason why the baby is at greater risk if born before this point.
practice_questions.marks: Description (up to 2 marks): the threshold of viability is the point at which a premature baby born at 24 weeks may survive with intensive neonatal support, as the lungs have reached sufficient development to have some chance of functioning (2 marks for a clear, accurate description; 1 mark for a basic statement). Explanation (up to 2 marks): before 24 weeks the lungs are too immature to sustain breathing independently or with ventilator support, because the air sacs (alveoli) and surfactant (the substance that prevents air sacs from collapsing) have not yet developed sufficiently (2 marks for a developed explanation with a specific reason; 1 mark for a vague statement). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A first-time mother is 30 weeks pregnant and has been offered a place on an NHS antenatal class. She is unsure whether to attend, as she feels she can find all the information she needs online.

Discuss the benefits and limitations of attending antenatal classes compared with using online resources to prepare for birth.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion. Benefits of classes: practical, interactive preparation (e.g. hands-on practice of nappy changing, breastfeeding positioning); real-time questions answered by a midwife; social networks formed with other parents due at the same time; partner involvement. Benefits of online resources: accessible at any time, often free, wide range of sources, can revisit information. Limitations of classes: may be infrequent, only one or two NHS sessions, may not match availability or learning style. Limitations of online: quality varies, risk of misinformation, no social element. A clear evaluative judgement should be reached.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two relevant points explained with reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One point with a brief reason.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A pregnant woman with a straightforward, low-risk pregnancy is deciding whether to give birth in hospital, at a midwife-led unit, or at home.

Evaluate the extent to which a midwife-led unit is the best choice for a low-risk pregnant woman who values minimal medical intervention but wants professional support during labour.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation arguing that for a low-risk woman who values minimal intervention, an MLU offers a homelike environment with midwife-led care, access to a birth pool and other non-pharmacological pain relief, lower rates of medical intervention than hospital, and evidence of comparable safety outcomes for mother and baby (Birthplace in England, 2011). Counter-arguments: an MLU cannot provide an epidural, continuous electronic foetal monitoring or emergency surgery; transfer to hospital (by ambulance) takes time and can be distressing if complications arise unexpectedly. A home birth may be even less interventional but carries a marginally higher risk for first-time mothers. A clear, substantiated judgement is required.
Secure (5–6 marks): At least two well-developed points with an attempt at a judgement and reference to the scenario.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but one-sided or without a clear judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic points with no evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a sign that labour has begun?
A) The baby drops lower in the pelvis at 36 weeks
B) Braxton Hicks contractions begin
C) The mucus plug is discharged from the cervix (a show)
D) The mother experiences heartburn
practice_questions.marks: C) The mucus plug is discharged from the cervix (a show) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two types of assisted delivery that a midwife or obstetrician may use if labour is not progressing.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two from: forceps delivery / ventouse (vacuum extraction) / episiotomy / elective or emergency caesarean section. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one disadvantage of using an epidural as a method of pain relief during labour.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying a disadvantage (e.g. 'an epidural can slow labour'). A second mark for development (e.g. 'this is because the reduced sensation makes it harder for the mother to push effectively during the second stage'). A third mark for a further development or linked consequence (e.g. 'which increases the likelihood of needing an assisted delivery using forceps or ventouse, adding further risk of tearing or bruising'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the second stage of labour. Give one example of what the midwife might do to support the mother during this stage.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): the second stage begins when the cervix is fully dilated at 10 centimetres and ends with the birth of the baby; the mother actively pushes the baby down through the birth canal during contractions (2 marks for a clear description of start, process and end; 1 mark for a partial answer).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, the midwife may coach the mother's breathing and pushing technique, monitor the baby's heart rate using a Doppler or CTG monitor, and prepare for crowning by asking the mother to stop pushing briefly to allow a controlled delivery of the head (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague answer). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Amina is 38 weeks pregnant and discussing her birth plan with her midwife. She is anxious about pain and wants to avoid medication that could affect her baby.

Discuss the pain relief options that would be most appropriate for Amina to consider.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion identifying at least two appropriate options (e.g. TENS — drug-free, safe, self-controlled, but limited to early labour; water/birthing pool — reduces pain and aids mobility, no drug transfer to baby; breathing and relaxation techniques — no risk, widely available, but may be insufficient for intense pain), explaining why each fits Amina's concern, and acknowledging a counter-argument (e.g. if pain becomes severe, she may need to reconsider; gas and air has minimal impact on the baby and could be a middle-ground option). A conclusion is reached that reflects Amina's stated priorities.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two relevant options identified and explained with some reference to Amina's situation.
Developing (2 marks): One option identified with brief explanation.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point with no development. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A first-time mother is considering whether to include a caesarean section in her birth plan as her preferred method of delivery.

Evaluate the advantages and disadvantages of a planned (elective) caesarean section compared with a natural vaginal birth.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): A balanced evaluation covering clear advantages of an elective caesarean (predictable timing, avoids prolonged labour, reduces risk of perineal trauma, preferred in certain medical conditions such as placenta praevia) and significant disadvantages (major surgery with longer recovery of 6–8 weeks, increased risk of infection and blood clots, baby misses beneficial exposure to vaginal bacteria, may affect breastfeeding establishment, future pregnancies carry scar tissue risks). The vaginal birth alternative is weighed (lower complication risk long-term, faster recovery, better breastfeeding outcomes) against its own uncertainties (unpredictable duration, potential for tearing, possibility of an emergency caesarean anyway). A substantiated judgement is reached — for example, that an elective caesarean is justified when there is a medical indication but is not recommended as a preference for convenience alone. Judgement must be supported with reasoning.
Secure (5–6 marks): At least two developed points on each side with an attempt at a conclusion.
Developing (3–4 marks): Points identified but largely one-sided or without a clear judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic, undeveloped points. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is NOT one of the five criteria assessed in the Apgar score?
A) Pulse
B) Grimace
C) Blood pressure
D) Respiration
practice_questions.marks: C) Blood pressure [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two conditions that the newborn blood-spot (heel-prick) test screens for.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: phenylketonuria (PKU) / congenital hypothyroidism / cystic fibrosis / sickle cell disease / MCADD / maple syrup urine disease / isovaleric acidaemia / glutaric aciduria type 1 / homocystinuria / hereditary tyrosinaemia type 1 (HT1). [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why it is important that the newborn hearing test is carried out as soon as possible after birth.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying the reason (e.g. 'to detect permanent hearing loss early'). A second mark for development (e.g. 'so that hearing aids or cochlear implants can be fitted before the critical period for language development'). A third mark for a further consequence (e.g. 'because children who receive early intervention develop far better communication skills than those identified later, reducing the impact on their education and social development'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what the Apgar score measures. Give one example of how the result of the Apgar score might affect the care given to the newborn.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): the Apgar score measures five aspects of the newborn's condition — Appearance (skin colour), Pulse (heart rate), Grimace (reflex response), Activity (muscle tone) and Respiration (breathing); each is scored 0–2 giving a maximum of 10 (2 marks for naming at least three criteria and explaining the scoring range; 1 mark for a partial answer).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, if a baby scores 3 at one minute, this indicates the baby requires immediate medical intervention such as resuscitation, airway clearance or oxygen administration; the medical team would act immediately rather than allowing the baby to be placed with the mother (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague response). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Mia's baby was born at 29 weeks and has been admitted to the Special Care Baby Unit.

Discuss the care and support that the SCBU will provide for Mia's baby and for Mia as the parent.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering baby-focused care (incubator for warmth, oxygen therapy or ventilation, tube feeding, phototherapy for jaundice, infection monitoring, specialist neonatal nurses and doctors) and parent-centred support (encouraged to visit, kangaroo care promoted, breastfeeding support, emotional support). A counter-perspective acknowledges the challenges: SCBU admission is emotionally distressing for parents, prolonged stays are isolating, and attachment can be harder to establish when the baby is in an incubator. Both aspects are developed with reasoning.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two relevant points identified with some reference to Mia's situation.
Developing (2 marks): One or two points identified without development.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Routine newborn checks are offered to all babies born in the UK in the days following birth.

Evaluate how effective these postnatal checks are in protecting the long-term health of the newborn.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Evaluates multiple checks and their specific impact — Apgar score enables immediate resuscitation decisions; heel-prick detects conditions such as PKU before irreversible brain damage; hearing test enables early intervention that dramatically improves language development; physical examination identifies hip dysplasia, cataracts and heart defects that are treatable if caught early. Argues these checks are highly effective because they target conditions where early treatment changes outcomes dramatically. Challenges this with counter-arguments: not all checks are equally reliable (false positives cause parental anxiety and unnecessary follow-up); some conditions screened for are very rare, raising questions about cost-effectiveness; social and environmental factors affecting long-term health (housing, poverty, parenting) are not addressed by neonatal checks. A substantiated judgement is reached — for example, that the checks are highly cost-effective and life-changing for the minority of babies affected, and the system is justified even accounting for false-positive rates.
Secure (5–6 marks): Two or more checks evaluated with advantages and limitations; a conclusion attempted.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but mainly one-sided; limited engagement with 'how effective'.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Lists checks with little evaluation. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes postnatal depression?
A) A low mood lasting 2–3 days after birth caused by hormonal changes
B) A persistent depression lasting weeks or months that requires professional support
C) A condition caused exclusively by a difficult labour
D) A normal stage all mothers experience in the first week
practice_questions.marks: B) A persistent depression lasting weeks or months that requires professional support [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two physical needs that must be met for a child to develop healthily.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: adequate nutrition (food) / warmth / rest and sleep / good hygiene / exercise and physical activity. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the health visitor supports a mother who is showing signs of postnatal depression.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying the health visitor's role (e.g. 'the health visitor screens for PND using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale'). A second mark for development (e.g. 'if the score indicates possible depression, the health visitor will discuss the mother's feelings and may refer her for talking therapy such as CBT or counselling'). A third mark for a further linked point (e.g. 'in severe cases the health visitor can refer to the perinatal mental health team, and early support is important because untreated PND can disrupt mother–baby bonding and affect the child's emotional development'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by the 'baby blues'. Give one way it differs from postnatal depression.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): the baby blues is a normal, temporary low mood that typically peaks around day 3–5 after birth as hormone levels — particularly oestrogen and progesterone — drop sharply; most mothers feel tearful, anxious or irritable but symptoms resolve within two weeks without treatment (2 marks for a description covering timing, cause and self-limiting nature; 1 mark for a partial answer).
Difference (up to 2 marks): postnatal depression, in contrast, persists beyond two weeks and lasts for months; it significantly impairs the mother's ability to function and requires professional intervention such as therapy or medication, unlike the baby blues which resolves on its own (2 marks for a clearly stated and explained difference; 1 mark for a basic contrast). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Aisha is a new mother who is finding it increasingly difficult to bond with her baby. She feels constantly anxious, has no appetite and rarely leaves the house.

Discuss the support available to Aisha and the possible effects on her baby if her condition goes untreated.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering support available (health visitor identification via EPDS, GP referral, talking therapies — CBT/counselling, antidepressant medication if appropriate, peer support groups, perinatal mental health team for severe cases) and the potential consequences for the baby if untreated (disrupted attachment, impaired bonding and emotional security, delayed language and social development due to reduced interaction and stimulation, risk of longer-term emotional and behavioural difficulties). Both sides developed with reasoning applied to Aisha's situation.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two relevant points with some reference to Aisha's situation.
Developing (2 marks): One or two points without development.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
A government health campaign claims that meeting children's emotional and social needs is just as important as meeting their physical needs for healthy development.

Evaluate this claim, drawing on your knowledge of the conditions required for child development.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Argues for the claim with evidence — attachment theory (Bowlby) shows that love and security form the foundation for emotional regulation and mental health; lack of stimulation leads to delayed language and cognitive development even in physically healthy children; socialisation is essential for school readiness. Challenges the claim with counter-arguments — physical needs are more immediately life-threatening; a malnourished or cold child cannot develop emotionally; in low-income families, meeting physical needs may be the greater challenge. Reaches a balanced, substantiated judgement — for example, that both categories are interdependent and neither can be ranked above the other for overall healthy development; the most vulnerable children are those who lack both. Judgement is explicit and supported.
Secure (5–6 marks): Two or more developed points on each side with an attempted conclusion.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but largely one-sided or without a clear judgement.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic, undeveloped points. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a warning sign that a child may have meningitis requiring immediate emergency action?
A) A blanching rash that fades when pressed with a glass
B) A mild fever that responds to paracetamol
C) A non-blanching rash that does not fade when pressed with a glass
D) Swollen parotid glands on one side of the face
practice_questions.marks: C) A non-blanching rash that does not fade when pressed with a glass [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two symptoms of chickenpox.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: fever / malaise / itchy rash of fluid-filled blisters / rash that starts on the chest or back and spreads / blisters that crust over. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit of the routine childhood immunisation schedule for the wider community.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying the benefit (e.g. 'immunisation contributes to herd immunity'). A second mark for development (e.g. 'when a high enough proportion of the population is immune, the disease cannot spread easily through the community'). A third mark for a further linked consequence (e.g. 'this protects those who cannot be vaccinated, such as newborns under 8 weeks, pregnant women and immunocompromised individuals, who are most at risk of serious complications if they contract the disease'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the signs and symptoms of measles. Give one reason why it is important that measles is treated promptly.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): measles begins with fever, cough, runny nose and red watery eyes; Koplik spots (white spots inside the cheeks) may appear 2–3 days before the rash; a red blotchy rash then spreads from the face down the body (2 marks for a description of at least three distinct symptoms including the rash; 1 mark for one or two symptoms only).
Reason (up to 2 marks): measles can lead to serious complications such as ear infection, pneumonia or, rarely, encephalitis (inflammation of the brain), any of which can cause permanent disability or death; prompt treatment reduces the risk of these complications developing (2 marks for a specific, explained reason; 1 mark for naming a complication without explanation). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
A parent tells their health visitor that they have decided not to have their child vaccinated against measles, mumps and rubella because they have read online that the MMR vaccine causes autism.

Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of the MMR vaccination that the health visitor might discuss with the parent.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering advantages (prevents three serious diseases; measles can cause encephalitis and death; mumps can cause orchitis and deafness; rubella is dangerous in pregnancy; MMR contributes to herd immunity, protecting babies too young to be vaccinated) and addressing the parent's concern with accurate counter-information (the MMR–autism claim came from a single retracted 1998 study by Wakefield, who lost his medical licence; large-scale studies of millions of children have found no link between MMR and autism; common side effects are minor and short-lived; anaphylaxis is extremely rare). A conclusion acknowledges that parental anxiety is understandable but that the evidence strongly supports vaccination.
Secure (3–4 marks): Two relevant points on each side with some reference to the scenario.
Developing (2 marks): One or two points without development.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Childhood immunisation programmes have significantly reduced the incidence of many serious diseases in the UK over the past 70 years.

Evaluate the effectiveness of the UK childhood immunisation schedule in protecting children's health.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Evaluates the schedule's effectiveness using evidence — smallpox eradication, near-elimination of polio in the UK, dramatic reduction in measles cases following MMR introduction, meningococcal B and C disease reduced since MenB/MenC vaccines. Argues the schedule is comprehensive, free, starts at 8 weeks and continues to age 14, and is informed by up-to-date epidemiological evidence. Challenges this by noting that effectiveness depends entirely on uptake — vaccine hesitancy driven by misinformation (MMR–autism myth) has caused measles outbreaks in areas with low uptake; some vaccines require booster doses to maintain immunity; no vaccine is 100% effective; and the schedule cannot protect against diseases for which no vaccine yet exists. Reaches a substantiated judgement — for example, that the schedule is highly effective overall but its protective value is undermined in communities with low uptake, making public trust and health visitor education as important as the vaccine itself.
Secure (5–6 marks): Two or more developed points on each side with an attempted conclusion.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but mainly one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic, undeveloped points. [8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following safety marks indicates a toy has been independently tested to a British Standard by the British Standards Institution?
A) UKCA mark
B) BSI Kitemark
C) Lion Mark
D) CE mark
practice_questions.marks: B) BSI Kitemark [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two ways a parent can reduce the risk of a young child being poisoned in the home.
practice_questions.marks: One mark each for any two of: store medicines and cleaning products in locked or child-resistant cupboards / keep products in their original containers / use child-resistant caps / remove or fence off poisonous garden plants / keep cosmetics and toiletries out of reach. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why a child should travel in a rear-facing car seat until they are at least 15 months old.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying the reason (e.g. 'rear-facing seats provide better protection in a frontal collision'). A second mark for development (e.g. 'because in a frontal crash the seat absorbs and spreads the impact force across the baby's back, head and neck together'). A third mark for a further linked point (e.g. 'young infants have disproportionately large and heavy heads relative to their neck muscles, making them vulnerable to serious head and spinal injury in a forward-facing seat during a collision; rear-facing seats significantly reduce this risk'). [3 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between the UKCA mark and the BSI Kitemark. Give one example of a product on which a parent might look for these marks.
practice_questions.marks:
Description (up to 2 marks): the UKCA mark is the legal minimum conformity marking indicating a product meets UK safety law requirements; the BSI Kitemark is a voluntary mark awarded by the British Standards Institution confirming the product has been independently tested to the relevant British Standard — providing a higher level of assurance than the UKCA mark alone (2 marks for a clear distinction covering legal status and level of testing; 1 mark for a basic distinction only).
Example (up to 2 marks): for example, when buying a stair gate, a parent should look for the BSI Kitemark confirming it has been tested to BS EN 1930, giving greater confidence in the gate's strength and reliability than the basic UKCA mark alone (2 marks for a specific, applied example; 1 mark for a vague example such as 'toys' without development). [4 marks total]

practice_questions.text:
Priya is decorating her home ready for the arrival of her first child. She wants to make both the living room and the kitchen as safe as possible for when the baby begins crawling and walking.

Discuss the safety measures Priya should take in her home to reduce the risk of accidents to her child.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): A balanced discussion covering at least two types of hazard in the relevant rooms (e.g. living room — socket covers or child-resistant sockets, corner and edge protectors on furniture, securing heavy furniture to walls, keeping cables tidy, fireguard on any open fire; kitchen — stair gate across door, cooker guard, turning pan handles inward, storing cleaning products in locked cupboard, keeping hot drinks out of reach) with specific prevention measures for each, and acknowledging limits (e.g. making an environment fully safe may not be feasible; supervision remains essential alongside physical safety measures; risks change as the child develops and new hazards emerge).
Secure (3–4 marks): Two relevant hazards identified with prevention measures, some reference to Priya's situation.
Developing (2 marks): One or two hazards with limited development.
Emerging (1 mark): A single relevant point. [6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Despite significant improvements in home safety products and public awareness campaigns, accidental injury remains the leading cause of death among children aged 1–14 in the UK.

Evaluate how effectively safety equipment and safety standards can reduce the risk of accidental injury to young children.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Evaluates specific equipment and its effectiveness (stair gates prevent stair falls; socket covers prevent electrocution; cooker guards and thermostat settings reduce scald risk; car seats reduce road fatality) and how safety standards (UKCA, BSI Kitemark, i-Size) ensure products are rigorously tested. Argues that these measures have demonstrably reduced specific accident types. Challenges this with evidence that equipment alone is insufficient — supervision is always required (a stair gate left open is useless; a child can still drown in 5 cm of water in a supervised moment); some safety products can give a false sense of security; lower-income families may be unable to afford high-quality safety equipment; accidents still occur because children's behaviour is unpredictable and hazard awareness changes with development. Reaches a substantiated judgement — for example, that safety equipment and standards are highly effective in reducing specific, predictable hazards but must be combined with active supervision and parental education to address the full range of risks, particularly as children become more mobile and independently exploratory.
Secure (5–6 marks): Two or more developed points on each side with an attempted conclusion.
Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points but mainly one-sided.
Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic, undeveloped points. [8 marks]
